question: Which statement best describes Semantic structure?
options: Semantic HTML names a page part by its purpose. A button is an action; a link moves somewhere. Screen readers use these built-in roles, and browsers provide keyboard behavior for many native controls. It is like using labeled doors instead of blank panels. Start with the correct element before adding ARIA. In practice, a native button responds to Space and Enter, while a clickable div needs extra keyboard work. In a real page, use a nav landmark for primary navigation so a screen-reader user can jump to it.

An accessible name tells assistive technology what a control does. A visible label is usually best for an input. Icon-only buttons need a clear name, such as “Close menu.” It is like putting readable text on a switch. Check that the name remains useful when read without nearby visual context. In practice, give a search field a visible label so its purpose remains clear after its placeholder disappears. In a real page, associate an input with a visible label that stays available after typing.

Every action should be reachable by keyboard, focus should be visible, and the order should match the task. It is like providing a continuous path through a building. Avoid custom controls that ignore standard keys. Test Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and Escape where they apply. In practice, a modal should move focus into its content and return focus to its trigger when closed. In a real page, when a dialog opens, place focus inside and return it after closing.

A screen reader announces page structure, names, and status to someone who cannot see the screen. Zoom and voice control are other tools people may use. It is like hearing a guide describe the building while walking through it. Test real interactions rather than relying only on automated scans. In practice, announce a save result with a status region without moving the person away from the form. In a real page, use a live status message for saved feedback without taking focus away.
